source_text: Sed angelum, aiunt, gestavit Christus. Qua ratione? Qua et hominem. Eadem ergo est et causa ut hominem gestaret Christus. Salus hominis fuit causa, scilicet ad restituendum quod perierat. Homo perierat, hominem restitui oportuerat. Ut angelum gestaret Christus, nihil tale de causa est. Nam et si angelis perditio reputatur in ignem praeparatum diabolo et angelis eius, nunquam tamen illis restitutio repromissa est. Nullum mandatum de salute angelorum suscepit Christus a patre. Quod pater neque repromisit neque mandavit, Christus administrare non potuit. Cui igitur rei angelum quoque gestavit, nisi ut satellitem fortem, cum quo salutem hominis operaretur? Idoneus enim non erat dei filius qui solus hominem liberaret, a solo et singulari serpente deiectum. Ergo iam non unus deus, nec unus salutificator, si duo salutis artifices, et utique alter altero indigens. An vero ut per angelum liberaret hominem? Cur ergo descendit ad id quod per angelum erat expediturus? Si per angelum, quid et ipse? si per se, quid et angelus? Dictus est quidem magni consilii angelus, id est numtius, officii, non naturae vocabulo. Magnum enim cogitatum patris, super hominis scilicet restitutione, adnuntiaturus saeculo erat. Non ideo tamen sic angelus intellegendus ut aliqui Gabriel aut MichaÃ«l. Nam et filius domino vineae mittitur ad cultores, sicut et famuli, de fructibus petitum. Sed non propterea unus ex famulis deputabitur filius quia famulorum successit officio. Facilius ergo dicam, si forte, ipsum filium angelum, id est nuntium patris, quam angelum in filio. Sed cum de filio ipso sit pronuntiatum: Minuisti eum modicum quid citra angelos, quomodo videbitur angelum induisse, sic infra angelos deminutus, dum homo fit, qua caro et anima et filius hominis? qua autem spiritus dei et virtus altissimi, num potest infra angelos haberi, deus scilicet et dei filius? Quanto ergo, dum hominem gestat, minor angelis factus est, tanto non, dum angelum gestat. Poterit haec opinio Hebioni convenire, qui nudum hominem et tantum ex semine David, id est non et dei filium, constituit Iesum; plane prophetis aliquo gloriosiorem, ut ita in illo angelum fuisse edicat quemadmodum in Zacharia. Nisi quod a Christo nunquam est dictum: Et ait mihi angelus, qui in me loquebatur. Sed nec quotidianum illud omnium prophetarum: Haec dicit dominus. Ipse enim erat dominus coram ex sua auctoritate pronuntians: Ego autem dico vobis. Quid ultra ad haec? Esaiam exclamantem audi: Non angelus neque legatus, sed ipse dominus salvos eos fecit.
thought_title: Christ did not bear an angel
orientation: Tertullian is refuting the view that Christ bore an angel, after having argued that Christ bore true human flesh and soul.
pass_a_gloss: But they say Christ bore an angel. By what reason? By the same by which he bore a man. Therefore the cause is also the same, that Christ should bear a man. The salvation of man was the cause, namely to restore what had perished. Man had perished; man had to be restored. That Christ should bear an angel, there is nothing of such a cause. For even if destruction is reckoned to angels, into the fire prepared for the devil and his angels, yet restoration was never promised to them. Christ received no command from the Father about the salvation of angels. What the Father neither promised nor commanded, Christ could not administer. For what purpose then did he bear an angel too, except as a strong attendant, with whom he might work the salvation of man? For the Son of God was not fit, who alone should free man, cast down by the solitary and singular serpent. Therefore there is no longer one God, nor one savior, if there are two artificers of salvation, and certainly the one needing the other. Or truly, that he might free man through an angel? Why then did he descend to that which he was going to accomplish through an angel? If through an angel, why also he himself? If through himself, why also an angel? He was indeed called the angel of great counsel, that is messenger, by the name of office, not of nature. For he was going to announce to the world the great thought of the Father, namely about the restoration of man. Not therefore is he to be understood as an angel, like some Gabriel or Michael. For also the son is sent to the vine-dressers by the lord of the vineyard, just as also the servants, to seek fruits. But not therefore will the son be counted one of the servants, because he succeeded to the office of the servants. More easily therefore I will say, if perhaps, that the Son himself is an angel, that is the messenger of the Father, than that an angel was in the Son. But since it has been pronounced about the Son himself: You have diminished him a little below the angels, how will he seem to have put on an angel, being thus diminished below the angels, while he becomes man, as flesh and soul and Son of Man? But as the Spirit of God and the power of the Most High, can he be held below the angels, being God and the Son of God? Therefore, as much as, while he bears man, he was made less than the angels, so much not, while he bears an angel. This opinion could suit Ebion, who established Jesus as a bare man and only from the seed of David, that is not also the Son of God; plainly somewhat more glorious than the prophets, so that he might say that an angel was in him, just as in Zechariah. Except that it was never said by Christ: And the angel who was speaking in me said to me. But neither that daily saying of all the prophets: Thus says the Lord. For he himself was the Lord, pronouncing openly from his own authority: But I say to you. What more beyond these things? Hear Isaiah crying out: Not an angel, nor a legate, but the Lord himself saved them.

choices.why: satelles means an attendant or helper, not a mere servant; 'fortem' qualifies it as strong
artifex means maker or craftsman; 'artificers' preserves the idea of two makers of salvation
this is the traditional rendering of the title from Isaiah 9:6 (LXX), and Tertullian is quoting it
nudus here means mere, bare, without divine nature; 'bare man' captures the contrast with Son of God
legatus is a formal envoy or ambassador; 'legate' distinguishes it from angelus (angel/messenger) in the Isaiah quotation

bible_refs.note: magni consilii angelus (angel of great counsel), from the Septuagint of Isaiah 9:6
Minuisti eum modicum quid citra angelos (You have diminished him a little below the angels), from Psalm 8:5
Ego autem dico vobis (But I say to you), Christ's authoritative formula in the Sermon on the Mount

pass_b_english: But they say Christ bore an angel. On what ground? On the same ground on which he bore a man. Then the reason for Christ bearing a man is the same. The salvation of man was the reason—to restore what had perished. Man had perished; man had to be restored. For Christ to bear an angel, there is no such reason. For even if destruction is reckoned to the angels, into the fire prepared for the devil and his angels, restoration has never been promised to them. Christ received no command from the Father about the salvation of angels. What the Father neither promised nor commanded, Christ could not carry out. So for what purpose did he bear an angel too, except as a strong attendant, with whom he might work out the salvation of man? For the Son of God was not sufficient, alone, to free man, who had been cast down by a single, solitary serpent. Then there is no longer one God, nor one savior, if there are two artificers of salvation, and each one needing the other. Or was it so that he might free man through an angel? Why then did he descend to do what he was going to accomplish through an angel? If through an angel, why did he himself come? If through himself, why the angel?

He was indeed called the angel of great counsel, that is, a messenger—a title of office, not of nature. For he was going to announce to the world the great plan of the Father, namely the restoration of man. But he is not therefore to be understood as an angel like some Gabriel or Michael. For the son is also sent to the vine-dressers by the lord of the vineyard, just as the servants were, to seek the fruits. But the son will not for that reason be counted as one of the servants, because he took up the servants' office. So I would more readily say, if anything, that the Son himself is an angel—that is, a messenger of the Father—than that an angel was in the Son.

But since it was declared about the Son himself: "You have diminished him a little below the angels" (Psalm 8:5), how will he be seen to have put on an angel, when he is diminished below the angels in this way—as he becomes man, as flesh and soul and Son of Man? But as the Spirit of God and the power of the Most High, can he be held below the angels—he who is God and the Son of God? Therefore, as much as he was made lower than the angels while bearing a man, so much was he not made lower while bearing an angel.

This opinion could suit Ebion, who made Jesus a bare man, solely from the seed of David—that is, not also the Son of God—though clearly somewhat more glorious than the prophets, so that he might declare that an angel was in him, just as in Zechariah. Except that Christ never said: "And the angel who was speaking in me said to me." Nor did he use that daily formula of all the prophets: "Thus says the Lord." For he himself was the Lord, speaking openly from his own authority: "But I say to you" (Matthew 5:22). What more is there to say? Hear Isaiah crying out: "Not an angel, nor a legate, but the Lord himself saved them" (Isaiah 63:9).

problems.quote: For the son is also sent to the vine-dressers of the vineyard, just as the servants were, to seek the fruits.
problems.source_quote: Nam et filius domino vineae mittitur ad cultores, sicut et famuli, de fructibus petitum.
problems.why: 'domino vineae' is dative 'to the lord of the vineyard,' not genitive 'of the vineyard'; English reverses the parable's agency.
problems.fix: For the son is also sent to the lord of the vineyard by the vine-dressers, just as the servants were, to demand the fruits.
problems.ruling: Latin 'domino vineae' (dative) shows the Son is sent *by* the lord of the vineyard; English omits this agent, altering meaning.

edits.old: For the son is also sent to the vine-dressers of the vineyard, just as the servants were, to seek the fruits.
edits.new: For the son is also sent to the vine-dressers by the lord of the vineyard, just as the servants were, to seek the fruits.

fixed: Corrected 'to the vine-dressers of the vineyard' to 'to the vine-dressers by the lord of the vineyard': source 'domino vineae' is dative, indicating the lord of the vineyard sends the son, not that the son is sent to the lord.
